relations.myth: Rival masters demand mutually exclusive service
relations.note: Mammon and God are personified as rival masters whom none can jointly serve.

relations.myth: Thomasine version of the rival-masters saying
relations.note: Mammon again appears as the master whose service is incompatible with God's.
A disputed later tradition attributes to Gregory an identification of Mammon with Beelzebub.
Jerome juxtaposes God and Mammon with the Pauline opposition between Christ and Belial.

relations.myth: Avaricious service opposes service to Christ
relations.note: Later commentators interpret allegiance to Mammon as incompatible with serving Christ.
Lucifer governs pride while Mammon governs avarice in the same classification.
Beelzebub governs envy while Mammon governs avarice; they share no narrative episode.
Satan governs wrath while Mammon governs avarice in the same classification.
Abaddon governs sloth while Mammon governs avarice; they share no narrative episode.
Belphegor governs gluttony while Mammon governs avarice; they share no narrative episode.
Asmodeus governs lust while Mammon governs avarice; they share no narrative episode.
Philotime, personification of worldly ambition, is presented as Mammon's daughter.

relations.myth: Guyon's trial in the Cave of Mammon
relations.note: Mammon tempts Guyon with gold, advancement, and Philotime's hand; Guyon refuses.
Mammon conducts Guyon through an underworld containing the garden of Proserpina.

relations.myth: Fallen host develops Hell and debates its future
relations.note: Mammon belongs to Satan's fallen host and advocates material development in Hell.

relations.myth: Construction of Pandemonium from Hell's mined ore
relations.note: Mammon leads ore extraction that enables Mulciber's construction of Pandemonium.
Modern comparisons equate Mammon with the classical wealth-god Plutus without ancient textual support.
